analysis.one_liner: Lets credit card and loan customers count a mailed payment by its postmark date, not when it arrives.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have counted a mailed payment as on-time from its postmark date, never left a House subcommittee and died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: When a customer mails a credit card or loan payment, it can take days to arrive. Under current Truth in Lending rules, the creditor counts the payment on the date it actually receives it, so slow mail can make an on-time payment look late and trigger a late fee or a higher interest rate. This bill would have required creditors to use the postmark date as the official payment date, unless the customer showed the payment was made even earlier. It was referred to a House subcommittee, where no further action was ever taken.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who mail their payments near a due date. If a payment is delayed in the mail, the postmark rule would protect them from late fees, penalty interest rate increases, and negative credit reporting caused by nothing more than postal delay.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a new section to the Truth in Lending Act requiring creditors, on any open or closed-end consumer credit account, to treat the postmark on the payment envelope as the date payment was made, unless the consumer shows the payment was made earlier.
This applies to grace periods offered by creditors, so a payment postmarked by the due date would count as on time even if it arrives after the due date.
The protection covers both revolving accounts like credit cards and installment loans, so it reaches the widest set of consumer credit customers.

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers and other consumer lenders, who would lose some late-fee revenue and penalty interest income that currently comes from payments delayed in the mail. They would also carry a small administrative burden in processing mailed payments with postmarks.
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit card issuers and consumer lenders

drawbacks.text: Creditors argue that they cannot be certain a payment actually contained the funds when postmarked, and that they bear the cost and risk of processing paper payments that may not clear until days after the postmark date.
The postmark rule only helps people who mail payments; it does nothing for the growing share of consumers paying electronically, and it does not cap late fees or penalty rates themselves.
The bill is two sentences long and contains no enforcement mechanism beyond the Truth in Lending Act's existing remedies, so compliance would depend largely on existing regulatory oversight.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to consumers is real but narrow: it fixes one specific way an on-time mailed payment can be treated as late, protecting people from fees and credit damage they did not cause. The cost to lenders is small, mostly the loss of a modest stream of late fees on mail-delayed payments. Honest supporters would concede it was a narrow fix in an era when electronic payment was beginning to reduce the underlying problem, and the bill as drafted offered no penalty or enforcement provision of its own.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Banking Committee's subcommittee on financial institutions and consumer credit, where nothing happened, and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. Andrew Jacobs Jr. introduced the Date of Payment Act on May 2, 1995, with one Democratic cosponsor.
The House referred it to the Committee on Banking and Financial Services on May 2, 1995, and three days later to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit.
No hearing, markup, or vote is recorded; the bill never left the subcommittee, and the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 without the bill advancing.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers and consumer lenders are better off because the bill died: they keep the ability to treat a mailed payment as late based on when it arrives rather than when it was postmarked, preserving the late fees that mail delays can generate.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Credit card issuers and consumer lenders

for.name: Rep. Andrew Jacobs Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Date of Payment Act and was its sole original sponsor.

against.name: House Banking and Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on May 2, 1995 and passed it to the subcommittee three days later; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled, and the bill died there at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the lone cosponsor were Democrats, but the bill attracted no floor opposition or votes, so its partisan shape was never tested.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and consumer lenders
industries.note: The bill would have ended their ability to charge late fees or raise rates when a mailed payment arrives after the due date despite being postmarked on time. Their financial interest in keeping the received-date rule ran against the interest of mailed-payment customers.
